toc.title: Let your body breathe the way it needs to

blocks.p: I got a question on YouTube asking how to use breath when working through this stuff. The comment mentioned a couple of named breathing techniques, something like "Polyvagal rebel breath," and "on the ropes," which I think is a boxing term. I have no idea what those are. If that's some new polyvagal hack, I'm not up to date on it. <!-- unclear: the technique names in the viewer's question are hard to make out in the audio -->
So the question, as I'll phrase it, is: how do you use your breath when looking inward, when trying to self-regulate, or when doing meditations?

blocks.h: Let your body breathe the way it needs to

blocks.p: My answer is that I would prefer people allow their body to breathe the way that it needs to breathe. I don't like prescribed breathing. I prefer my clients not count their breaths, or count how many seconds they're breathing in, or out, or holding it for. To me, that adds a layer of thought that is not necessary and potentially unhelpful.
If someone needs that kind of containment, that's fine. That's probably more of a coping skill, and I have no problem with that whatsoever.

But if the intention is to feel into what's happening within us, I would recommend we reduce our cognitions as much as we can. Thoughts are going to come in and out. That's normal, that's fine. But counting is, I believe, an unnecessary, abstract thought that is not needed for that moment.

To connect with what's happening within us, we anchor into safety: mindfully anchored in safety, feeling safety within us. Then we tiptoe into defensive activation as we are open and curious and ready to. And we only stay with defensive activation as our safety state allows us to.
So how does breath come into this?

When I lead people through a cohort or a skills practice, I will use one intentional, bigger breath here and there. Even that, I believe, is kind of artificial, but it's fine. It serves as an anchoring point.

It's not "breathe in for three, hold it for four, and then out for twelve," or whatever the heck. I'm just making up numbers. It's not like that. It's just: take in a bigger breath than your previous one, and let it out slowly if you can. That's really it. All that does is help to balance out defensive activation and bring us back to the body if needed. I think that can be a great way to re-anchor.

If you're doing this by yourself, you really have to be aware of defensive activation that might be getting to be too much. Then maybe use that one intentional breath to re-anchor into safety, and either pause the practice or continue feeling into defensive activation.

Other than that, your body knows how much oxygen it needs, so let it breathe the way that it needs to breathe. That's what I recommend. There's no system here, no hack, no gimmick. Your body knows how to breathe, so let it breathe. And while it's breathing, just be mindful of it.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: The way I work, I teach people to be mindful of their breath and the way it naturally wants to breathe, maybe taking that one intentional breath.

Beyond that, we're looking at what safety feels like in the body at a very deep level, and describing what it feels like. We're also looking at stuck defensive activation that's just kind of lingering there. And we're being mindful of what I call obstacles: other things that pop up.

For example, someone might be anchored in safety and trying to feel into what immobility or collapse feels like, and then all of a sudden there's a spike of, we'll say, anxiety. So we have to be mindful of these little spikes and notice them as they come up.

There are a lot of pieces we're mindful of, and breath is one of them. But I would get concerned about someone trying to count their breathing, because now we're worried about "am I counting it right?" That is not where I want people's mindfulness to be.

I don't want people to be in a state of evaluating whether they're doing it right or wrong. I would much rather they be curious about what's naturally there, what's naturally coming up. Using our cognitions to count, or to gauge whether we're doing it right or wrong, seems to me like a step in the wrong direction.

Again, if someone's in a heightened state and they need to contain their defensive activation, I think that's perfectly fine. I don't have a problem with that whatsoever. But that's different from a meditative self-regulation exercise. That's a different thing.

There's no hack in how I approach this. We're connecting with the present moment as much as we can, for what it is. It's a very simplified approach, but I'm not saying it's easy. It focuses on small steps and skill mastery. I don't expect someone to do something like pendulation unless they can do a few things before that: learning the Polyvagal Theory, building their safety state, and then building the self-regulation skills one by one, mastering each before moving on to the next.
